articles.author: Pedro Dropa
articles.description:
I am an engineering manager and the thing I could never keep current was not the code, it was the shape of the org. Who sits where, what each team is carrying, what it costs. That lived across a spreadsheet, a wiki page and some Slack threads, and it was stale the moment I finished assembling it.
Squado is one canvas with alliances, tribes and squads and the people on them. Drag someone into another squad and pick whether they transfer or stay on both. Vacation, split allocations and open seats show on the faces. Set hourly rates by role once and cost rolls up per squad, tribe and alliance. OKRs attach to the squads that own them, and the ceremony calendar flags the overlaps.
The link goes straight into a fictional fintech org, 10 squads and the people on them, no signup and no account. It is read-only for visitors, so you can click into everything but not change it.
Stack is React, React Flow, Fastify, Prisma and Supabase. The canvas query is cached in Redis for 30 seconds, which is what keeps a 50KB payload feeling instant for everyone looking at the same org.
I built it alone and I am mostly curious where the model breaks for orgs that are not shaped like this. If you do not run anything resembling squads and tribes, I would like to hear what you do run.
There is a full demo with no signup: https://app.squado.io/demo
https://squado.io
articles.title: Squado - Your engineering org on one live canvas

A badge that never expires is not a control. It is a spare key under the mat. On 27 October in Atlanta, IBM put a name on the agent and tied that name to a credential that is supposed to die. Keep that. Leave the kill switch in the keynote where it is. It is still a preview. Do not clap for a control you cannot press on a system that is already live.
Vault already does the useful thing for ordinary applications. It mints a secret for one job. Then the secret expires. Agent Identity, generally available today, is the row that secret has to match: who owns the agent, whether it is still allowed to work, and what it may touch. articles.description:
I fine-tuned a pretrained reranker, verified that its weights changed, reloaded the selected checkpoint, and ran a controlled comparison with the original model.
The measured ranking gain on the held-out synthetic slice was zero.
That result was useful. It showed that the training and evaluation path executed while giving me no reason to claim an improvement. The slice contained three questions, only two of them answerable. Both rerankers reached nDCG@5 of 1.0 on those two answerable questions.
This is a local, AI-assisted experiment in progress. Real-domain fine-tuning and a sealed real held-out comparison have not been completed. Human review of generated answers is also pending. The current evidence supports a working experimental pipeline and a tied result on a tiny synthetic fixture.
